_comment: Hand-written Animal Friday lines (DOJP-52), keyed by the English vernacular name GBIF reports for the species in birds.json. House style: start with the bird's name, 1-2 sentences, kid-friendly, exclamation marks welcome. A species with no entry here is never narrated. Lines rotate by ISO week.
Northern Cardinal: Northern Cardinals are bright red all over, like a little flying fire engine, and they sing their cheer-cheer-cheer song even in the snow!
Northern Cardinals do not fly south for the winter, so a red cardinal on a white snowy branch is one of the prettiest sights in the whole sky!
Blue Jay: Blue Jays are bright blue with a pointy crest on their head, and they can copy the scream of a hawk to scare other birds away from the feeder!
Blue Jays love acorns so much they bury thousands of them every autumn, and the ones they forget grow into brand new oak trees!
American Robin: American Robins have a round orange belly and hop across lawns tilting their heads, listening for worms wriggling under the grass!
American Robins lay eggs of such a beautiful blue that the color is named after them: robin's egg blue!
American Crow: American Crows are some of the cleverest birds alive, and they can remember a person's face for years and years!
American Crows gather in enormous flocks at bedtime, sometimes thousands of them cawing together in one big noisy tree!
Mourning Dove: Mourning Doves make a soft, sad-sounding coo that people often mistake for an owl, and their wings whistle when they take off!
Mourning Doves can drink without lifting their heads, sucking up water like a straw while every other bird has to tip its beak to the sky!
House Sparrow: House Sparrows are tiny brown chatterboxes that live almost everywhere people do, from farms to the busiest city streets!
House Sparrows love a dust bath, flopping about in dry dirt to clean their feathers like a bird-sized bubble bath without the bubbles!
European Starling: European Starlings look black from far away, but up close their feathers shimmer purple and green like oil on a puddle!
European Starlings fly together in gigantic swirling clouds called murmurations that twist and turn across the sky like one giant creature!
Common Starling: Common Starlings look black from far away, but up close their feathers shimmer purple and green like oil on a puddle!
Common Starlings fly together in gigantic swirling clouds called murmurations that twist and turn across the evening sky like one giant creature!
Red-winged Blackbird: Red-winged Blackbirds are glossy black with a bright red and yellow patch on each shoulder, like a little soldier wearing badges!
Red-winged Blackbirds sing conk-la-ree from the tops of reeds, and the males will dive-bomb anything that comes too close to their nest, even people!
Canada Goose: Canada Geese fly in a big V shape so each bird gets a lift from the one in front, taking turns at the hard job up at the point!
Canada Geese honk loudly to each other while they fly, and they can travel more than a thousand miles in a single day of flying!
Mallard: Mallards are the classic duck: the dads have a shiny green head and the mums are speckled brown, and only the mums do the loud quacking!
Mallards have waterproof feathers thanks to a special oil they spread with their beaks, so water just rolls right off them!
Song Sparrow: Song Sparrows sing a sweet tune that starts with three clear notes and ends in a trill, and each one has its own favorite version of the song!
Song Sparrows are little streaky brown birds that hop along the ground pumping their tails up and down as they fly!
Black-capped Chickadee: Black-capped Chickadees say their own name when they call: chick-a-dee-dee-dee, and the more dees they add, the more danger is about!
Black-capped Chickadees hide thousands of seeds in autumn and can remember every single hiding place all winter long!
Carolina Chickadee: Carolina Chickadees are tiny puffballs with a black cap and bib, and they can hang upside down from twigs to grab bugs other birds miss!
Carolina Chickadees say chick-a-dee-dee-dee to warn their friends about danger, and more dees means a scarier visitor!
Tufted Titmouse: Tufted Titmice have a pointy grey crest and huge dark eyes, and they are bold enough to pluck fur straight off a sleeping dog to line their nests!
Tufted Titmice whistle peter-peter-peter so loudly you would never guess the singer is smaller than your hand!
Downy Woodpecker: Downy Woodpeckers are the smallest woodpeckers in North America, and they drum on trees so fast their heads become a blur!
Downy Woodpeckers have a special spongy skull that works like a bike helmet, so all that hammering never gives them a headache!
Red-bellied Woodpecker: Red-bellied Woodpeckers have a bright red stripe down the back of their head and a zebra-striped back, and they can stick their tongue out two inches to grab bugs!
Red-bellied Woodpeckers wedge nuts into cracks in tree bark and hammer them open like a tiny feathered carpenter!
Carolina Wren: Carolina Wrens are little brown birds with a bold white eyebrow, and they sing teakettle-teakettle-teakettle louder than birds ten times their size!
Carolina Wrens build nests in the funniest places, like old boots, flower pots, and even the pocket of a coat left on a porch!
House Finch: House Finches have a rosy red head and chest, and the redder a dad finch is, the more the mums like him!
House Finches sing a long cheerful warble, and they love a backyard feeder so much they often arrive in a whole chattering family!
American Goldfinch: American Goldfinches are bright lemon yellow in summer, and they fly in a bouncy up-and-down pattern as if riding an invisible roller coaster!
American Goldfinches wait until late summer to nest so they can line it with soft thistle fluff, and they feed their babies seeds instead of bugs!
Dark-eyed Junco: Dark-eyed Juncos are called snowbirds because they appear in backyards just as winter arrives, flashing white tail feathers when they fly!
Dark-eyed Juncos spend most of their time hopping on the ground, kicking through leaves to find seeds like tiny grey gardeners!
White-breasted Nuthatch: White-breasted Nuthatches walk headfirst down tree trunks, upside down, which no other backyard bird can do!
White-breasted Nuthatches jam seeds into bark and hatchet them open with their beaks, which is exactly how they got the name nut-hatch!
Northern Mockingbird: Northern Mockingbirds can copy the songs of dozens of other birds, and some even learn to mimic car alarms and squeaky gates!
Northern Mockingbirds sing all day and sometimes all night long, especially under a bright full moon!
Turkey Vulture: Turkey Vultures soar for hours without flapping, wobbling side to side on wings held up in a V, and they can smell their dinner from a mile away!
Turkey Vultures have bald red heads and are nature's clean-up crew, tidying away anything that has stopped moving!
Red-tailed Hawk: Red-tailed Hawks have a rusty red tail and a scream so fierce that movies use their call whenever any eagle appears on screen!
Red-tailed Hawks can spot a mouse from the top of a tall tree, then drop like a stone at over a hundred miles an hour!
Bald Eagle: Bald Eagles are not bald at all: their heads are covered in snow white feathers, and their nests can weigh as much as a small car!
Bald Eagles have eyesight so sharp they can spot a fish swimming underwater from high up in the sky!
Great Blue Heron: Great Blue Herons stand as tall as a six-year-old and can freeze completely still for ages before spearing a fish with lightning speed!
Great Blue Herons fly with their long necks folded into an S shape and their legs trailing behind like a flying pterodactyl!
Ring-billed Gull: Ring-billed Gulls have a neat black ring around their yellow beak, and they are the gulls most likely to be eyeing up your chips in a car park!
Ring-billed Gulls can drink salty seawater thanks to special glands above their eyes that squeeze the salt back out!
Rock Pigeon: Rock Pigeons are the city pigeons you see everywhere, and they can find their way home from hundreds of miles away using the Earth's magnetic field!
Rock Pigeons were the original mail carriers, flying secret messages for armies long before there were telephones or the internet!
Common Grackle: Common Grackles look plain black until the sun hits them, and then their heads flash bright blue and purple like a shiny marble!
Common Grackles strut around on the ground like they own the place, and they can crack open hard acorns with a special ridge inside their beak!
Eastern Bluebird: Eastern Bluebirds are sky blue on top and rusty orange underneath, like a little piece of sunset sitting on a fence post!
Eastern Bluebirds nearly vanished once, but people built thousands of special nest boxes for them and now they are back everywhere!
Ruby-throated Hummingbird: Ruby-throated Hummingbirds beat their wings more than fifty times a second, and they are the only birds that can fly backwards!
Ruby-throated Hummingbirds weigh less than a coin, yet every autumn they fly nonstop across the whole Gulf of Mexico without landing!
Anna's Hummingbird: Anna's Hummingbirds have a head and throat that flash hot pink in the sun, and they hum so fast their wings become invisible!
Anna's Hummingbirds perform a dive that reaches sixty miles an hour, and at the bottom their tail feathers make a loud chirp!
California Scrub-Jay: California Scrub-Jays are bright blue with a grey back, and they hide so many acorns that they help plant whole forests of oak trees!
California Scrub-Jays are clever enough to spy on other jays hiding food, then sneak back later and steal it!
Steller's Jay: Steller's Jays are deep blue with a tall black crest, and they are the noisiest, boldest birds at any mountain picnic table!
Steller's Jays can imitate the scream of a hawk perfectly, which sends every other bird at the feeder scattering!
Common Raven: Common Ravens are the biggest songbirds in the world, and they are clever enough to solve puzzles and play games just for fun!
Common Ravens do somersaults and barrel rolls in the air for no reason except that it looks like a wonderful time!
Northern Flicker: Northern Flickers are woodpeckers that prefer to hop around on the ground eating ants, and they flash bright yellow or red under their wings when they fly!
Northern Flickers drum on metal chimneys and street signs in spring to make the loudest possible announcement that this is their patch!
American Kestrel: American Kestrels are the smallest falcons in North America, and they can hover in one spot in mid-air like a tiny helicopter!
American Kestrels can see ultraviolet light, which lets them follow the glowing trails that mice leave behind in the grass!
Killdeer: Killdeer are shorebirds that nest on gravel and even flat roofs, and they shout their own name, kill-deer, as they fly!
Killdeer pretend to have a broken wing, flopping and crying, to lure foxes away from their eggs, then zoom off perfectly healthy!
Osprey: Ospreys dive feet-first into the water to grab fish, then turn the fish head-forward in their talons so it flies like a tiny torpedo!
Ospreys build enormous stick nests on top of poles and platforms, and they come back to the very same nest year after year!
Great Horned Owl: Great Horned Owls have feathery tufts like horns and a hoot so deep you can feel it, and they can turn their heads almost all the way around!
Great Horned Owls fly in complete silence thanks to soft fringed feathers, so a mouse never hears them coming!
Common Wood-Pigeon: Common Wood Pigeons are big plump pigeons with a white patch on their necks, and their wings clap loudly together when they burst out of a tree!
Common Wood Pigeons coo a sleepy five-note song that sounds a bit like my toe bleeds Betty, over and over again!
Eurasian Magpie: Eurasian Magpies are black and white with a long tail that shimmers green and blue, and they are one of the only animals that recognise themselves in a mirror!
Eurasian Magpies chatter like a rattle, and an old rhyme says one for sorrow, two for joy, so always look out for a second one!
Carrion Crow: Carrion Crows are all black from beak to toe, and they are clever enough to drop nuts on roads so passing cars crack them open!
Carrion Crows caw three or four times in a row, bobbing their whole body as if the shout takes real effort!
European Robin: European Robins have a bright orange chest and sing all through the winter, which is why they appear on so many Christmas cards!
European Robins are so friendly to gardeners that they will hop right up to a spade, waiting for a juicy worm to be dug up!
Eurasian Blue Tit: Eurasian Blue Tits are tiny blue and yellow acrobats that hang upside down from twigs and bird feeders to reach the tastiest bits!
Eurasian Blue Tits can lay more than ten eggs in one nest, and the parents catch hundreds of caterpillars a day to feed all those hungry chicks!
Great Tit: Great Tits have a black head, white cheeks, and a yellow belly with a black stripe, and their teacher-teacher song is the sound of spring!
Great Tits are such quick learners that in some towns they figured out how to peck open milk bottle tops to drink the cream!
Eurasian Blackbird: Eurasian Blackbirds sing one of the most beautiful songs of any bird, a slow flute-like tune from the rooftops at dawn and dusk!
Eurasian Blackbird dads are jet black with a bright orange beak, while the mums are brown, and both hop across lawns listening for worms!
Common Blackbird: Common Blackbirds sing one of the most beautiful songs of any bird, a slow flute-like tune from the rooftops at dawn and dusk!
Common Blackbird dads are jet black with a bright orange beak, while the mums are brown, and both hop across lawns listening for worms!
Black-headed Gull: Black-headed Gulls wear a chocolate brown hood in summer that vanishes in winter, leaving just a little dark smudge behind each eye!
Black-headed Gulls follow tractors across fields in noisy flocks, snapping up worms turned over by the plough!
Herring Gull: Herring Gulls are the big noisy seaside gulls with a red spot on their beak that their chicks tap to ask for dinner!
Herring Gulls stamp their feet on wet grass to trick worms into thinking it is raining, and up they come!
European Herring Gull: European Herring Gulls are the big noisy seaside gulls with a red spot on their beak that their chicks tap to ask for dinner!
European Herring Gulls stamp their feet on wet grass to trick worms into thinking it is raining, and up they come!
Eurasian Wren: Eurasian Wrens are one of the tiniest birds in Europe, yet their song is so loud it can be heard right across a wood!
Eurasian Wren dads build several nests and let the mum choose her favorite, like a tiny feathered estate agent!
Dunnock: Dunnocks are quiet brown birds that shuffle about under hedges, flicking their wings in a nervous little wave!
Dunnocks are often called hedge sparrows, but they are not sparrows at all, and they sing a sweet hurried song from the top of a bush!
Common Chaffinch: Common Chaffinches have a pink chest, a blue-grey cap, and bright white wing bars that flash when they fly!
Common Chaffinches sing a rattling song that ends with a flourish, and birds in different places sing it with their own accent!
European Goldfinch: European Goldfinches have a bright red face and golden wing bars, and a flock of them is called a charm!
European Goldfinches have beaks so pointy they can pull seeds out of prickly thistles and teasels that other birds cannot reach!
Eurasian Jackdaw: Eurasian Jackdaws are small crows with pale silvery eyes and a grey hood, and they love to nest in chimneys and church towers!
Eurasian Jackdaws say their own name, jack, and they pair up for life, often cuddling side by side on a rooftop!
Western Jackdaw: Western Jackdaws are small crows with pale silvery eyes and a grey hood, and they love to nest in chimneys and church towers!
Western Jackdaws say their own name, jack, and they pair up for life, often cuddling side by side on a rooftop!
Common Moorhen: Common Moorhens have a bright red and yellow beak and huge green feet, and they bob their heads as they paddle across ponds!
Common Moorhen chicks from the first brood help feed their younger brothers and sisters later in the summer!
Eurasian Coot: Eurasian Coots are round black waterbirds with a white forehead, and they have the strangest lobed toes, like leaves on the end of each foot!
Eurasian Coots are famously grumpy, splashing and chasing any other bird that paddles too close to their patch of pond!
Red Kite: Red Kites have a forked tail like a swallow and glide on wings as wide as a grown-up is tall, twisting their tail to steer!
Red Kites almost disappeared from Britain, but they were brought back and now hundreds soar over towns, sometimes swooping for a dropped sandwich!
Common Buzzard: Common Buzzards soar in slow circles over fields, mewing like a cat, and they are the most common bird of prey in Britain!
Common Buzzards can spot a beetle crawling in the grass from high above, and they will happily walk about a field hunting for worms!
Pied Wagtail: Pied Wagtails are little black and white birds that never stop wagging their long tails up and down, even when standing still!
Pied Wagtails gather in huge roosts on winter nights, sometimes hundreds of them snuggled in one tree in the middle of a shopping centre!
White Wagtail: White Wagtails are little black, white and grey birds that never stop wagging their long tails up and down, even when standing still!
White Wagtails run after insects along riverbanks and car parks with quick little steps, like a wind-up toy!
Long-tailed Tit: Long-tailed Tits are tiny pink and white fluffballs with a tail longer than their body, and they travel in chattering family gangs!
Long-tailed Tits build a stretchy nest out of moss, spider silk and up to two thousand feathers, and it grows as the chicks get bigger!
Eurasian Collared-Dove: Eurasian Collared Doves are pale pinkish grey with a thin black collar on the back of their neck, and they coo a three-note song all day long!
Eurasian Collared Doves spread across all of Europe in just fifty years, and now they are one of the most common doves around!
Australian Magpie: Australian Magpies are black and white with a glorious warbling song, and they can remember the faces of people they like and people they do not!
Australian Magpies will swoop at cyclists and walkers in spring to protect their nests, so Australians wear funny hats with eyes on the back!
Rainbow Lorikeet: Rainbow Lorikeets are painted in every color of the rainbow, with a blue head, orange chest and green wings, and they screech like a crowd at a party!
Rainbow Lorikeets have a brush on the end of their tongue for lapping up flower nectar, and they can get a little wobbly from fermented fruit!
Noisy Miner: Noisy Miners are grey birds with a yellow beak and a bright yellow patch behind the eye, and they live up to their name by never, ever being quiet!
Noisy Miners live in big bossy gangs that chase away every other bird, even eagles, from their patch of trees!
Sulphur-crested Cockatoo: Sulphur-crested Cockatoos are big white parrots with a bright yellow crest that pops up like a crown when they get excited!
Sulphur-crested Cockatoos can live for eighty years, and they have learned to open rubbish bin lids with their beaks to look for snacks!
Galah: Galahs are rose pink and grey parrots that gather in huge noisy flocks, and they love hanging upside down from wires in the rain!
Galahs pair up for life, and in Australia calling someone a galah means they are being a bit silly, which these playful birds often are!
Laughing Kookaburra: Laughing Kookaburras make a call that sounds exactly like a crowd of people laughing, and the whole family joins in to greet the sunrise!
Laughing Kookaburras are the biggest kingfishers in the world, and instead of fish they swoop down on lizards, mice and even snakes!
Willie Wagtail: Willie Wagtails are little black and white birds that wag their tail from side to side and are brave enough to pester eagles!
Willie Wagtails sing a sweet song that Australians say sounds like sweet pretty creature, even in the middle of the night!
Magpie-lark: Magpie-larks are black and white birds also called peewees, because that is exactly what they call out, pee-wee, pee-wee!
Magpie-larks build neat bowl-shaped nests out of mud, and the mum and dad sing duets together, taking turns note by note!
Australian White Ibis: Australian White Ibises have a long curved black beak and bald black head, and city folk call them bin chickens for their love of rubbish bins!
Australian White Ibises were once only wetland birds, but they have moved into parks and city squares and now strut around like they own them!
Crested Pigeon: Crested Pigeons have a thin black spike of feathers on their head, and their wings whistle loudly as they take off to warn their friends of danger!
Crested Pigeons bob their heads and fan their tails in a funny bowing dance when they want to impress another pigeon!
Little Corella: Little Corellas are small white cockatoos that gather in flocks of hundreds, screeching and tumbling through the air like feathered confetti!
Little Corellas are playful tricksters that hang upside down, slide down roofs, and chew on anything they can get their beaks on!
Pied Currawong: Pied Currawongs are big black birds with bright yellow eyes, and their ringing curra-wong call echoes through the trees!
Pied Currawongs are clever enough to take apart a berry to get at the seed inside, and they move down from the mountains to town every winter!
Welcome Swallow: Welcome Swallows have a forked tail and a rusty orange face, and they zip over fields and ponds snapping up insects in mid-air!
Welcome Swallows got their name because sailors knew that spotting one meant land, and home, was close by!
Superb Fairywren: Superb Fairywren dads turn an electric sky blue in spring, while the rest of the year they are plain brown like the mums!
Superb Fairywrens hop about with their tails held straight up, and the dads bring the mums yellow flower petals as presents!
Red Wattlebird: Red Wattlebirds have little red dangly bits on their cheeks called wattles, and they make a call that sounds like a loud cough!
Red Wattlebirds are big honeyeaters that guard their favorite flowering tree fiercely, chasing off any bird that tries to sneak a sip!
Silver Gull: Silver Gulls are the seagulls of Australia, with bright red legs and beak, and they will steal a chip right out of your hand at the beach!
Silver Gulls can drink seawater, squeezing the salt out through their noses, so they never need a freshwater drink!
Australian Raven: Australian Ravens are big glossy black birds with white eyes, and their long wailing call sounds like a baby crying, aaah-aaah-aaaaah!
Australian Ravens have shaggy throat feathers that puff out when they call, and they are clever enough to open lunch boxes!
Masked Lapwing: Masked Lapwings have a bright yellow face mask and sharp yellow spurs on their wings, and they nest right in the middle of sports fields!
Masked Lapwings will swoop and shriek at anyone who walks near their eggs, which are so well camouflaged they look like stones!
Eastern Spinebill: Eastern Spinebills have a long curved beak like a needle for sipping nectar, and their wings make a whirring sound as they hover at flowers!
Eastern Spinebills are tiny honeyeaters with a black and white head and a rusty orange belly, zipping between flowers like a hummingbird!
Spotted Dove: Spotted Doves have a black patch on the back of their neck covered in white spots, like a tiny checkered scarf!
Spotted Doves coo a gentle three-note song from rooftops and wires, and they bow and puff up their chest to show off!
Common Myna: Common Mynas are brown birds with a yellow mask around their eyes, and they strut about on their yellow legs like busy little bosses!
Common Mynas are talented mimics that can copy other birds, and some pet mynas even learn to say words!
Grey Butcherbird: Grey Butcherbirds sing one of the loveliest songs in Australia, a rolling flute-like tune, and the whole family joins in the chorus!
Grey Butcherbirds have a hooked beak and hang their food on thorns to save it for later, which is how they got their name!
Barn Swallow: Barn Swallows have a deeply forked tail and a shiny blue back, and they swoop low over fields catching bugs on the wing!
Barn Swallows build cup-shaped nests out of mud, carrying hundreds of tiny mouthfuls of it to stick together under a barn roof!
Cedar Waxwing: Cedar Waxwings look like they are wearing a silky tan suit with a black mask and a yellow-tipped tail, as smooth as a bird can be!
Cedar Waxwings pass berries down a row from beak to beak until one of them finally eats it, like a polite game of pass the parcel!
Blue-gray Gnatcatcher: Blue-gray Gnatcatchers are tiny grey birds that flick their long tails side to side to scare up bugs, like a wagging feathered finger!
Blue-gray Gnatcatchers build a neat little cup nest covered in lichen that looks just like a bump on the branch!
Chipping Sparrow: Chipping Sparrows have a neat rusty cap and sing a long dry trill that sounds like a tiny sewing machine!
Chipping Sparrows used to line their nests with horsehair, and they will still happily use fur combed out of a dog!
Gray Catbird: Gray Catbirds are slate grey with a black cap, and they got their name because their call sounds exactly like a cat mewing!
Gray Catbirds copy other birds' songs and string them together into one long, rambling tune that can last for ten minutes!
Brown-headed Cowbird: Brown-headed Cowbirds never build a nest; instead they sneak their eggs into other birds' nests and let them do all the babysitting!
Brown-headed Cowbirds got their name from following herds of cattle and bison, snapping up the insects the big animals stir up!
Pileated Woodpecker: Pileated Woodpeckers are crow-sized with a flaming red crest, and they are the bird that Woody Woodpecker was based on!
Pileated Woodpeckers chisel enormous rectangular holes in dead trees looking for ants, leaving wood chips piled up below like a lumberjack!
Hairy Woodpecker: Hairy Woodpeckers look like a bigger version of the Downy Woodpecker, with a beak as long as their head for hammering deep into bark!
Hairy Woodpeckers follow Pileated Woodpeckers around and snack on the insects left behind in their giant holes!
Eastern Phoebe: Eastern Phoebes are plain grey-brown flycatchers that pump their tails up and down and say their own name, fee-bee, over and over!
Eastern Phoebes love to build their mud nests under bridges and porch roofs, and they come back to the same spot every spring!
Black Phoebe: Black Phoebes are sooty black with a snow white belly, and they sit by ponds and pools flicking their tails before darting out to snap a fly!
Black Phoebes build nests of mud stuck to walls under bridges and eaves, and they often come back to the same one for years!
Yellow-rumped Warbler: Yellow-rumped Warblers have a bright yellow patch on their rump that earned them the nickname butter-butts!
Yellow-rumped Warblers can digest waxy berries that other warblers cannot, so they can stay far north in winter when their cousins fly south!
Wild Turkey: Wild Turkeys can fly short bursts at fifty miles an hour, and they roost high up in trees at night where foxes cannot reach them!
Wild Turkey dads puff up all their feathers and fan their tails like a giant bronze peacock, gobbling so loudly it carries a mile!
Double-crested Cormorant: Double-crested Cormorants dive underwater to chase fish, then stand on rocks with their wings spread wide to dry off like a washing line!
Double-crested Cormorants have bright turquoise eyes and an orange throat, and they can swim with just their snaky neck poking out of the water!
Snow Goose: Snow Geese fly in flocks so huge that when they land on a field it looks like a snowstorm has fallen on just that one spot!
Snow Geese travel thousands of miles between the Arctic and the south every year, honking in a chorus that can be heard from far below!
Common Loon: Common Loons have a haunting wailing call that echoes across northern lakes, and they can dive more than two hundred feet down to chase fish!
Common Loons have legs set so far back on their bodies that they can barely walk on land, but underwater they swim like torpedoes!
Great Egret: Great Egrets are tall snow white herons with a yellow dagger beak, and they grow long lacy feathers on their backs in spring!
Great Egrets stalk through shallow water in slow motion and then strike like a snake to grab a fish or a frog!
Brown Pelican: Brown Pelicans fold their wings and plunge headfirst into the sea from high up, scooping up fish in a pouch that holds three buckets of water!
Brown Pelicans glide in a line just inches above the waves, riding the air pushed up by the water like surfers of the sky!
Sandhill Crane: Sandhill Cranes are tall grey birds with a red cap that dance together, leaping and bowing with their wings spread wide!
Sandhill Cranes make a rattling bugle call so loud it can be heard from two miles away as they fly in V shapes overhead!
Peregrine Falcon: Peregrine Falcons are the fastest animals on the planet, diving at over two hundred miles an hour, faster than a Formula One car!
Peregrine Falcons now nest on skyscrapers and bridges in big cities, treating them like the cliffs they would use in the wild!
Cooper's Hawk: Cooper's Hawks are speedy forest hawks that zip between trees chasing smaller birds, and they often visit backyard feeders for a snack!
Cooper's Hawks have long tails that work like rudders, letting them twist and turn through thick branches at full speed!
Arctic Tern: Arctic Terns fly from the top of the world to the bottom and back every single year, the longest journey of any animal on Earth!
Arctic Terns see more daylight than any other creature, because they spend summer at both the North and the South Pole!
Atlantic Puffin: Atlantic Puffins have a rainbow striped beak and can carry more than a dozen little fish crosswise in it at the same time!
Atlantic Puffins are nicknamed sea parrots, and they flap their wings four hundred times a minute to fly, zooming over the waves!
Mute Swan: Mute Swans are huge white birds with an orange beak, and they are strong enough to break a grown-up's arm with a wing, so admire them from a distance!
Mute Swans are not really mute at all: they hiss and grunt, and their wings make a loud whistling throb as they fly overhead!
Grey Heron: Grey Herons stand as still as statues at the edge of ponds, then stab down with their dagger beak faster than you can blink!
Grey Herons fly with their necks tucked in and their long legs trailing behind, flapping slowly like a prehistoric pterodactyl!
Common Kestrel: Common Kestrels hover in one spot over fields with their tails fanned out, holding their heads perfectly still while hunting for voles!
Common Kestrels can see ultraviolet light, which shows up the glowing trails that mice leave in the grass!
Eurasian Sparrowhawk: Eurasian Sparrowhawks dash through gardens at top speed, twisting between fences and bushes to surprise small birds at the feeder!
Eurasian Sparrowhawk mums are much bigger than the dads, nearly twice the size, and they have fierce yellow eyes!
Common Swift: Common Swifts eat, drink and even sleep while flying, and a young swift can stay in the air for two whole years without landing!
Common Swifts scream around rooftops in screeching gangs on summer evenings, and their tiny legs are so weak they can barely walk!
Common House-Martin: Common House Martins have a bright white rump and build mud nests under the eaves of houses, carrying over a thousand beakfuls of mud!
Common House Martins swoop high in the sky catching flying insects, and they fly all the way to Africa for the winter!
Song Thrush: Song Thrushes sing each phrase of their song two or three times over, as if making sure you heard it properly!
Song Thrushes smash snails on a favorite stone called an anvil to crack them open, leaving a pile of broken shells behind!
Eurasian Nuthatch: Eurasian Nuthatches are the only birds in Britain that can walk headfirst down a tree trunk, and they plaster mud around their nest hole to shrink the door!
Eurasian Nuthatches wedge nuts into bark and hammer them open with their beak, which is exactly how they got their name!
Eurasian Treecreeper: Eurasian Treecreepers are tiny streaky brown birds that spiral up tree trunks like a mouse, poking their curved beak into cracks for bugs!
Eurasian Treecreepers always climb up a tree and never down, so when they reach the top they fly to the bottom of the next one and start again!
Coal Tit: Coal Tits are tiny birds with a black cap and a white patch on the back of their neck, and they hide seeds all over the place for later!
Coal Tits are so small that they can squeeze into holes other birds cannot, and they love to flit around the tops of fir trees!
Greenfinch: Greenfinches are chunky olive green finches with flashes of yellow on their wings, and they wheeze a buzzy call from the treetops!
Greenfinches do a special butterfly flight in spring, flapping slowly in circles above the trees to show off!
European Greenfinch: European Greenfinches are chunky olive green finches with flashes of yellow on their wings, and they wheeze a buzzy call from the treetops!
European Greenfinches do a special butterfly flight in spring, flapping slowly in circles above the trees to show off!
Rook: Rooks are big black crows with a bare grey face, and they nest together in noisy treetop villages called rookeries!
Rooks walk about fields in a waddle, probing the ground for grubs, and they are clever enough to use sticks as tools!
Common Gull: Common Gulls have a gentle face, a yellow beak and greenish legs, and they paddle their feet on grass to bring worms to the surface!
Common Gulls follow the plough in winter like all good gulls, but in summer they nest beside wild lochs and moorland pools!
Lesser Black-backed Gull: Lesser Black-backed Gulls have slate grey wings and bright yellow legs, and they will travel a long way inland to raid a landfill!
Lesser Black-backed Gulls nest on flat city rooftops nowadays, which they treat just like the clifftops they used to use!
Great Spotted Woodpecker: Great Spotted Woodpeckers are black and white with a splash of red, and their drumming on a dead branch is the sound of early spring!
Great Spotted Woodpeckers have a tongue so long it wraps around the inside of their skull, perfect for hooking grubs out of deep holes!
Green Woodpecker: Green Woodpeckers have a red cap and a loud laughing call called a yaffle, and they spend most of their time on the ground eating ants!
Green Woodpeckers have a sticky tongue that stretches out four inches to slurp up ants from deep inside their nests!
Eurasian Jay: Eurasian Jays are pinkish brown with a flash of electric blue on their wings, and their screech is one of the loudest sounds in the woods!
Eurasian Jays bury thousands of acorns each autumn and remember where most of them are, planting many a new oak tree with the ones they forget!
Stock Dove: Stock Doves are shy blue-grey pigeons with a shiny green patch on their neck, and they nest inside hollow trees!
Stock Doves are often mistaken for city pigeons, but their gentle cooing comes from quiet farmland and old woods!
Eurasian Oystercatcher: Eurasian Oystercatchers are black and white with a long bright orange beak like a carrot, and they pipe loudly as they fly along the shore!
Eurasian Oystercatchers use their beak to hammer or pry open mussels, and each one learns a favorite technique from its parents!
Northern Lapwing: Northern Lapwings have a long wispy crest and shimmering green wings, and they tumble through the air calling pee-wit, pee-wit!
Northern Lapwings nest right out in the open on fields, and the parents pretend to be hurt to lure foxes away from the eggs!
Common Snipe: Common Snipes have a beak as long as their body for probing deep in the mud, and they zigzag away at top speed when startled!
Common Snipes make a strange bleating sound by spreading their tail feathers in a dive, which people used to think was a sky goat!
Common Redshank: Common Redshanks have bright orange-red legs and are called the sentinels of the marsh because they shout a warning before anyone else!
Common Redshanks bob their heads nervously and pipe loudly as they fly off, showing a flash of white on their wings!
Meadow Pipit: Meadow Pipits are small streaky brown birds that flutter up into the sky singing and then parachute slowly back down to the grass!
Meadow Pipits are the favorite foster parents of the cuckoo, who sneaks an egg into their nest and leaves them to raise the giant chick!
Redwing: Redwings are small thrushes with a bold cream eyebrow and a rusty red patch under each wing, and they arrive in autumn from the far north!
Redwings fly south by night, and on still autumn evenings you can hear their thin seep calls as they pass overhead in the dark!
Fieldfare: Fieldfares are big colorful thrushes with a grey head and a speckled chest, and they chatter in noisy flocks across winter fields!
Fieldfares defend their nests by dive-bombing intruders and splattering them with droppings, which really does work!
Hooded Crow: Hooded Crows are grey with a black head, wings and tail, as if a crow put on a grey jumper!
Hooded Crows drop shellfish from high up onto rocks to crack them open, and they are clever enough to pull up fishing lines for the catch!
